messages.subject: [statnet_help] Learning ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Dear teachers:
      I have learned statnet package for several month, here I have some questions to ask:
      1.Which term of ERGM should be chosen for interaction of two network covariates ( e.g. an advice network and a support network in a group)? Particularly, I want to know can entrainment effect and exchange effect between two networks be modeled in the same ERGM regression?
      2.An comparison between two variable coefficients can be tested by "Wald test". In the ERGM regression, how to comprare two coefficients ( one for reciprocity, the other for transitivity) by Wald test?
     Thank you for answering my questions in advance.
My best wishes!


Wang (Hopefield) Xi
Sun Yat sen University of China

messages.body_plain:
Hi --

Welcome to the statnet help list!

It looks like you've got a pretty complex model specification, so what I 
would suggest is starting more simply:  e.g., the dyad independent terms 
first, then adding the dyad dependent terms one at a time to see if a 
specific term produces this degeneracy, and if not, adding combinations 
of the terms to see when it happens.  Keep an eye on all of the 
coefficients as you progress, to see if there's a strong correlation among 
some of the terms.  That can be a sign of overfitting/colinearity.

In particular, for adding combinations of DD terms, I'd start with the 
degree related terms, then add balance, then add each of the gw*sp terms 
in sequence.

It's also worth starting with alpha=0 for the gw*sp terms.

Hope this helps.  Let us know what happens.

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The research team that I am working with has begun working with ERGMs on large enough data sets that we are looking into building a new computer for running ERGMs. When testing the effects of running multiple cores in parallel, I discovered a strange behaviour: adding more cores increased the runtime, rather than decreased it.
I used code of the following style:
start.time1 <- Sys.time()
model_1 <- ergm(DATA ~ edges +
                  gwdsp(0.7, fixed = T),
                control = control.ergm(seed=42,
                                       parallel = 1,
                                       parallel.type = 'PSOCK'))
summary(model_1)
dev.off()
end.time1 <- Sys.time()
time.taken1 <- end.time1 - start.time1
start.time2 <- Sys.time()
model_2 <- ergm(DATA ~ edges +
                  gwdsp(0.7, fixed = T),
                control = control.ergm(seed=42,
                                       parallel = 2,
                                       parallel.type = 'PSOCK'))
summary(model_2)
dev.off()
end.time2 <- Sys.time()
time.taken2 <- end.time2 - start.time2
I continued this for 1 to 8 cores on my test machine and found that the runtimes increased for each core added.
However, when I tried something similar with the flormarriage data set, I found a marked decrease with the addition of the second core, holding steady afterwards, and then a gradual increase at around 6-8 cores.
Am I performing my tests incorrectly? Is this a feature of data? If looking to run ERGMs in a reasonable time, what steps can we take to improve performance, or what kind of features should we look for in a machine beyond enough RAM to store the data and higher clock speeds?

Thanks,
Alexander Graham
Master's of Sociology Candidate
University of Waterloo
